clinicalPearls: Thyroid nodules are common and usually benign, but the central task is to identify the minority that are malignant
Initial evaluation begins with a serum TSH; a suppressed value points towards an autonomously functioning (usually benign) nodule and warrants a radionuclide scan
Ultrasound characterises nodules and stratifies malignancy risk, with features such as marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, and a taller-than-wide shape raising concern
Fine-needle aspiration is the key diagnostic test, with results reported using standardised cytology categories that guide management
Hot (functioning) nodules on scanning rarely harbour malignancy, so aspiration is generally directed at non-functioning nodules
History of childhood neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer, rapid growth, hoarseness, or fixed hard nodules increase suspicion of cancer
Molecular testing of indeterminate cytology samples can refine the risk of malignancy and help avoid unnecessary surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid nodules arise from focal proliferation of follicular cells and may be colloid nodules, adenomas, cysts, areas of thyroiditis, or carcinomas. Autonomously functioning nodules develop constitutive activation of thyroid hormone production, often through activating mutations of the TSH-receptor or G-protein signalling pathway, suppressing TSH and appearing 'hot' on scanning. Malignant nodules result from oncogenic alterations (for example in the MAPK pathway) driving unregulated growth, and their behaviour ranges from indolent differentiated cancers to aggressive anaplastic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Parathyroid or other neck mass mimicking a thyroid nodule
additionalInvestigations: Serum TSH as the first-line test
Thyroid ultrasound to characterise the nodule and assess cervical lymph nodes
Radionuclide thyroid scan when TSH is suppressed
Molecular marker testing for indeterminate cytology
Serum calcitonin when medullary carcinoma is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging, hard, or fixed nodule
New hoarseness or vocal cord palsy suggesting recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
History of head and neck irradiation or family history of thyroid cancer or MEN syndromes
Compressive symptoms such as dysphagia or stridor
reference.prognosis: Most nodules are benign and can be followed conservatively, and even most malignant nodules are differentiated cancers with an excellent prognosis after treatment, though anaplastic and some medullary cancers carry a poor outlook.
pitfalls: Proceeding to biopsy before checking TSH and missing an autonomous nodule that does not need aspiration
Relying on nodule size alone rather than sonographic risk features to decide on aspiration
Falsely reassuring the patient after a non-diagnostic aspirate without repeating sampling
Overlooking calcitonin measurement when clinical features suggest medullary carcinoma
